prompt: An agency promises your client the #1 spot on Google. What does Google say about that?
options: No one can guarantee a #1 ranking on Google
Only Google Partners can guarantee it
It is possible with a paid Search plan
It is fine as long as they put it in the contract

prompt: Does a site have to sign up for Search Console to appear in Google Search results?

Yes, unregistered sites are never shown
Only online stores must sign up
Only if the site is less than a year old
explanation: Search Console is a free tool to see and improve how Google views your site, but you do not need it to be included in Search.

source.title: Google: Get started with Search Console

prompt: Which page title follows Google's advice for a page title?
options: A short, descriptive title unique to that page
The same title on every page of the site
The main keyword repeated several times in a row

source.title: Google: Influencing your title links

options: Allowed if the sites are popular
explanation: Google's spam policies list buying or selling links for ranking purposes as link spam.

source.title: Google: Spam policies for Google web search

prompt: What does Google mean by "people-first" content?
options: Made mainly for people, not to game rankings
Content that always names and quotes real people
Content written in the first person
Content posted on social media first

source.title: Google: Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content

source.title: Google: Spam policies for Google web search

prompt: What extra step does Google require for a page to appear in AI Overviews?
options: None: no special optimization is needed
Adding a special AI text file to the site
Paying for an AI Overviews listing
explanation: Google says there are no additional requirements or special optimizations. The page just needs to be indexed and eligible to show with a snippet.

source.title: Google: AI features and your website

prompt: With mobile-first indexing, which version of a site does Google use for indexing and ranking?

source.title: Google: Mobile-first indexing best practices

prompt: E-E-A-T is Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness and Trust. Which does Google call most important?
explanation: Google's helpful content guide says that of these aspects, trust is most important.

source.title: Google: Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content

prompt: You improved a site today. How long does Google say changes can take to show in Search?
options: From a few hours to several months
Never, unless you pay for a recrawl

source.title: Google: SEO Starter Guide

prompt: A cafe owner asks: can I pay Google to crawl my site more often or rank it higher?
options: No, Google doesn't accept payment for that
Yes, through a Search Console upgrade
Yes, if you also run Google Ads

source.title: Google: In-depth guide to how Google Search works

prompt: How does Google find most new pages on the web?
options: By reading every new domain registration
By following links from pages it knows
From lists that site owners email Google
By checking social media profiles daily

source.title: Google: SEO Starter Guide

prompt: A competitor's site is full of spammy tricks. What does Google suggest you do about it?
options: Copy their tricks to keep up
Pay Google to push them down
File a search quality user report
Leave bad reviews on their profile
explanation: Google invites anyone who spots a site breaking its spam policies to send a search quality user report. Copying the tricks only puts your own site at risk.

source.title: Google: Spam policies for Google web search

prompt: What is image alt text for, in plain words?
options: A setting that makes the image load faster
A watermark that stops image copying
A caption that only shows on mobile
A short text that describes the image
explanation: Alt text is a short, descriptive piece of text that explains how an image relates to your content. Write it for people, in plain words.

source.title: Google: SEO Starter Guide

prompt: An online shop reuses the same product text on a few pages. Is that against Google's spam rules?
options: No, duplicate content isn't a spam violation
Yes, it triggers an automatic penalty
Yes, the whole site gets removed
Only if the pages are less than a year old
explanation: Google says duplicate content isn't a violation of its spam policies and won't cause a manual action. It's just inefficient, so unique text is still the better choice for shoppers.

source.title: Google: SEO Starter Guide

prompt: Where does Google mainly get the short text (snippet) shown under a search result?
explanation: Snippets are primarily created from the page content itself. Google sometimes uses the meta description when it describes the page better, so write a clear, unique one for each page.

source.title: Google: Control your snippets in search results

prompt: A client's traffic dips after a Google core update. What does Google say these updates are?
options: Penalties for sites that broke the rules
Tests that only affect new websites
Broad changes, not aimed at specific sites
Manual reviews done by Google staff
explanation: Core updates are broad changes Google makes several times a year, and they don't target specific sites. Focus on lasting improvements for users rather than quick fixes.

source.title: Google: Google Search's core updates and your website

prompt: An old SEO checklist says to fill in the "meta keywords" tag. Does Google Search use it?
options: Yes, it's a top ranking signal
Yes, but only for local businesses
Only when it lists 50 keywords or more
No, Google Search doesn't use it
explanation: Google Search doesn't use the keywords meta tag at all. Spend that time on clear titles and genuinely useful content instead.

source.title: Google: SEO Starter Guide

prompt: A client buys a domain stuffed with keywords to rank higher. What does Google say?
options: Domain keywords alone have hardly any effect
It guarantees a spot on the first page
It's the strongest ranking signal there is
It's required to rank for that phrase
explanation: Google's SEO Starter Guide says keywords in a domain name or URL path alone have hardly any effect on ranking. Pick a name that works for your brand instead.

source.title: Google: SEO Starter Guide

prompt: For Google Discover, how wide does Google suggest your large images should be?

source.title: Google: Get on Discover

prompt: A florist adds keywords in white text on a white background so only Google sees them. What is this?
options: A safe way to sneak in extra keywords
Fine if the words match the page
Only a problem on mobile pages
explanation: Text hidden from visitors but meant for search engines is hidden text spam. Write words people can actually see and use.

source.title: Google: Spam policies for Google web search

prompt: In plain words, what are the three stages Google Search works in?
explanation: Google finds pages (crawling), understands and stores them (indexing), then shows them for searches (serving). Not every page makes it through all three.

source.title: Google: In-depth guide to how Google Search works

prompt: What is the name of the program that fetches web pages for Google Search?
explanation: Googlebot is Google's crawler: the program that visits and downloads pages so Google can learn about them.

source.title: Google: In-depth guide to how Google Search works

prompt: A cheese shop links to its tasting guide. Which link text does Google call too generic?
explanation: Link words should tell people and Google what's on the other side. Phrases like "Read more" or "Click here" say nothing.

source.title: Google: Link best practices for Google

prompt: A pet shop uploads a kitten photo. Which file name does Google say is the better choice?
explanation: A short, descriptive file name gives Google a small clue about what the image shows. Camera default names give none.

source.title: Google: Google image SEO best practices

prompt: You open the Performance report in Search Console. What time span does it show by default?
explanation: The report opens on the last three months of clicks and impressions. You can change the date range with the filters at the top.

source.title: Search Console Help: Performance report (Search results)

prompt: A yoga studio is making its little site icon (favicon) for search results. What shape must it be?
explanation: Google needs a square favicon, at least 8x8 pixels, and suggests going bigger than 48x48 so it looks sharp.

source.title: Google: Define a favicon to show in search results

prompt: Search Console shows a manual action on a client's site. Who made that decision?
explanation: A manual action means a real person at Google checked the site and found pages breaking the spam policies.

source.title: Search Console Help: Manual Actions report

prompt: A recipe blog's pop-up covers the recipe. Google's page experience checklist asks you to avoid what?
options: Pages that run longer than 1,000 words
More than three photos a page
explanation: Google's page experience questions include avoiding intrusive interstitials: pop-ups that block what visitors came for.

source.title: Google: Understanding page experience in Google Search results

prompt: A site shows Google a page about recipes but shows real visitors a casino page. What is this called?
explanation: Showing search engines one thing and people another, to manipulate rankings, is cloaking. It's a clear spam policy violation.

source.title: Google: Spam policies for Google web search

prompt: Google talks about "YMYL" topics, like health or money. What does YMYL stand for?

source.title: Google: Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content

prompt: You just launched a brand new website. What does Google call the best first step to get it indexed?

explanation: Asking Google to index your homepage in Search Console gets crawling started. Good internal links help it find the rest.

source.title: Search Console Help: Page indexing report

prompt: An FAQ page hides answers in click-to-open sections (accordions). Is that hidden text spam?
options: Yes, any hidden text counts as spam
Only if over half is hidden
No, accordions and tabs are fine
Yes, unless it's a mobile page
explanation: Hiding text to trick search engines is spam, but normal design like accordions and tabs that visitors can open is fine.

source.title: Google: Spam policies for Google web search

prompt: A shop buys a former charity's expired domain to sell on the old site's reputation. What is this?
explanation: Buying an expired domain mainly to ride its old rankings with unrelated content is expired domain abuse.

source.title: Google: Spam policies for Google web search

prompt: A trusted medical site hosts an unrelated third-party "best casinos" page to rank it. What is this?

source.title: Google: Spam policies for Google web search

prompt: A plumber makes dozens of near-identical city pages that all funnel visitors to one page. What is it?
explanation: Lots of thin pages made just to catch searches and push people to one destination are doorways. Build real pages for real places you serve.

source.title: Google: Spam policies for Google web search

prompt: Google shows a different title for your page than you wrote. Can you ask Google to change it by hand?
options: Yes, through a Google support chat
Yes, for a small yearly fee
No, Google can't do that per site
Only if you also run Google Ads
explanation: Google can't hand-edit title links for single sites. Your best lever is a clear, accurate title on the page itself.

source.title: Google: Influencing your title links in search results

prompt: A shop moves to a new domain. Should it redirect all of its old pages to the new home page?
options: Yes, that keeps all of the old rankings
Yes, but only the old blog posts
No, just delete the old pages
No, send each to a matching new page
explanation: Redirect each old page to its closest new match. Pointing everything at the home page confuses visitors and Google.

source.title: Google: Site moves with URL changes

prompt: No time to write page descriptions (snippet text) for every page? Which does Google say to cover first?
explanation: If you must prioritize, write descriptions for your most important pages, like the home page and the ones people visit most.

source.title: Google: Control your snippets in search results

prompt: A bakery is moving to a new domain and also wants a full redesign. What does Google advise?
options: Do everything together on one day
Change only one thing at a time
Pause the old site for a month
explanation: Splitting big changes apart makes problems easier to spot and fix, and keeps the move smoother in Search.

source.title: Google: Site moves with URL changes

prompt: A dentist wants a private page kept out of Google. Is blocking it in robots.txt (crawler rules) enough?
options: Yes, that's the official way to do it
No, block indexing or add a password
explanation: Robots.txt mainly manages crawler traffic. To keep a page out of Google, block indexing with noindex or put it behind a password.

source.title: Google: Introduction to robots.txt

explanation: The Removals tool is temporary. For a permanent fix, remove or update the page, or block it from indexing.

source.title: Search Console Help: Removals and SafeSearch reports Tool

prompt: Your client sees their site ranked differently than you do for the same search. What does Google say?
options: Results vary by time, place and device
One of you is being penalized
Google ranks paying customers a bit higher
explanation: Search results depend on when, where and on what device someone searches, plus their recent history, so two people can see different results.

source.title: Search Console Help: Performance report (Search results)

source.title: Google Search Central Blog: HTTPS as a ranking signal

options: It's the single top ranking factor
It's a score in Search Console
It isn't a specific ranking factor
It only applies to news sites
explanation: E-E-A-T describes qualities Google's many signals try to reward. It isn't a single factor or score you can directly push up.

source.title: Google: Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content

options: Only if you're a verified owner
No, it's a hint, not a rule
explanation: Google weighs your preferred page as a strong hint, but it may still pick a different main (canonical) page for various reasons.

source.title: Google: What is canonicalization

prompt: A shop switches from http to https on the same domain. Does it need the Change of Address tool?
options: No, Google says not to use it then
Yes, it's required for every site move
Yes, or rankings reset to zero
explanation: Change of Address is for moving to a new domain or subdomain. For an http to https switch, follow the site move steps and Google figures it out.

source.title: Search Console Help: Change of Address tool

options: The fixed pages come back right away
No partial return to search results
The penalty is cut in half
It lifts on its own in 30 days

source.title: Search Console Help: Manual Actions report

prompt: Which page counts as a video "watch page" in Google's eyes?
options: A blog post reviewing an embedded video
A category page listing many videos
A page mainly showing one video
A product page with a 360 video

source.title: Google: Video SEO best practices

source.title: Google: Google image SEO best practices

options: Every time someone sees your ad on a web page
A valuable action, like a purchase or a call
Changing your ad into another language
Moving budget from one campaign to another

source.title: Google Ads Help: About conversion measurement

options: Where your business pin sits on Maps
Which hours of the day your ads run
The places where your ads can appear
Which websites link to your shop
explanation: Location targeting shows your ads in the places you pick: countries, regions, cities or a radius around a spot.

source.title: Google Ads Help: About targeting geographic locations

source.title: Google Ads Help: About keyword matching options

source.title: Google Ads Help: About manager accounts

source.title: Google Ads Help: About negative keywords

prompt: You give a responsive search ad several headlines. What does Google Ads do with them?
options: Shows every headline at once, every single time
Uses only the first one you typed
Tests different mixes and learns what works
Asks searchers to vote for a favourite
explanation: Google Ads combines your headlines and descriptions in different ways and learns which combinations perform best.

source.title: Google Ads Help: About responsive search ads

prompt: Under Google's ad policies, which ad claim is not allowed?
options: The real price you charge for the service you sell
An unlikely result sold as what most people get

source.title: Google Advertising Policies: Misrepresentation

prompt: You set an average daily budget. On a busy day, what can Google Ads do?
options: Spend more than it, up to a daily limit
Never spend a cent over it
Ask you to approve the extra spend by email first
explanation: Daily spend varies. On some days a campaign can go over its average daily budget, but never past its daily spending limit.

source.title: Google Ads Help: About average daily budgets

prompt: Quality Score has an 'ad relevance' part. What does it look at?
options: How much you bid per click
How well your ad matches the search intent
How many years your Google Ads account has existed
How many ads your campaign has
explanation: Ad relevance is how closely your ad matches the intent behind a search. Quality Score is a diagnostic, not an auction input.

source.title: Google Ads Help: About Quality Score

prompt: With cost-per-click (CPC) bidding, when do you actually pay Google?
options: Every time your ad is shown
A flat fee once a month
explanation: CPC means you pay for clicks, not for views. Your ad can appear many times at no cost until someone clicks it.

source.title: Google Ads Help: Cost-per-click (CPC): Definition

explanation: Ad scheduling lets you pick the days and hours your ads can show. Without it, campaigns run all day, every day.

source.title: Google Ads Help: About ad scheduling

prompt: Is there an extra fee just to add assets like sitelinks or callouts to your ads?
options: Yes, a monthly fee per asset
Yes, a fee each time one shows
explanation: Assets cost nothing to add. You only pay the usual price when someone clicks your ad.

source.title: Google Ads Help: About assets

source.title: Google Ads Help: About call assets

prompt: A bot keeps clicking your ad. What does Google say about paying for invalid clicks?
options: You pay full price for each one
You won't be charged for them
You pay half price for each one

source.title: Google Ads Help: Invalid clicks

prompt: You set a maximum CPC of $2. What does a single click usually cost you?
explanation: Your max CPC is a ceiling, not a price tag. The actual cost per click is often lower than what you set.

source.title: Google Ads Help: Cost-per-click (CPC): Definition

prompt: Which campaign type reaches YouTube, Search, Gmail and Maps from one single campaign?

source.title: Google Ads Help: About Performance Max campaigns

prompt: A craft brewery wants to run ads. How do Google's ad policies treat alcohol?

source.title: Google Advertising Policies Help: Google Ads policies

prompt: How often does Google calculate your Ad Rank?
options: Only when you change your bid
explanation: Ad Rank is worked out fresh in every auction, so your ad's position can change from one search to the next.

source.title: Google Ads Help: About Ad Rank

prompt: One viewer clicks your headline, a sitelink and a call button on one ad view. Most clicks you pay for?

source.title: Google Ads Help: About assets

prompt: A shoe shop runs Shopping ads. What does Google use to decide where those ads show?

source.title: Google Ads Help: About Shopping ads

prompt: A yoga studio wants to run a Video campaign. What do they need to do first?
explanation: Video campaigns use a video that already lives on YouTube, so upload it there before you build the campaign.

source.title: Google Ads Help: Choose the right campaign type

prompt: A bakery sets up a Smart campaign. Besides writing an ad and a budget, what do they choose?
explanation: Smart campaigns keep things simple: you write the ad, pick keyword themes and set a budget, and Google handles the rest.

source.title: Google Ads Help: How Smart campaigns work

prompt: Your new ad shows 'Poor' ad strength. Can it still be shown to people?
options: No, not until it reaches Good
explanation: Ad strength is advice to help you improve, not a gate. A 'Poor' ad can still run, but better assets usually help.

source.title: Google Ads Help: About Ad Strength for responsive search ads

prompt: Google Ads gives each keyword a Quality Score. What scale is it measured on?
explanation: Quality Score runs from 1 to 10 and is shown for each keyword. Higher means your ads and pages look more useful.

source.title: Google Ads Help: About Quality Score for Search campaigns

prompt: You never touch the ad schedule setting. When can your ads show?
explanation: Campaigns are set to 'All day' by default. Add an ad schedule only if you want to limit the days or hours.

source.title: Google Ads Help: About Ad Scheduling

prompt: Google's tip for writing callout text: which version is better?
options: Our shipping is free for you
explanation: Short, punchy phrases work best for callouts. 'Free shipping' says it all in two words.

source.title: Google Ads Help: About callout assets

prompt: A hotel adds structured snippets listing its amenities. Can people click on them?
options: Yes, each opens its own page
Only when seen on a phone
explanation: Structured snippets just show extra info, like a list of amenities. Use sitelinks if you want extra clickable links.

source.title: Google Ads Help: About structured snippet assets

prompt: You just created a new ad. How long does Google's review usually take?
explanation: Most ads are reviewed within one business day. Complex cases can take a little longer, so plan launches ahead.

source.title: Google Ads Help: About the ad review process

prompt: Your ad's status says 'Disapproved'. What does that mean for the ad?
options: It shows with a warning label
explanation: A disapproved ad can't run at all. Fix the issue or appeal, and the ad gets reviewed again.

source.title: Google Ads Help: About the ad review process

prompt: A website sells fake documents like doctors' notes. Can it advertise on Google?
options: Yes, if it targets adults only
Yes, on the Display Network only
explanation: Google doesn't allow ads for things that help people cheat or deceive, like fake documents or academic cheating services.

source.title: Google Advertising Policies: Google Ads policies

prompt: A customer wants to see what other ads a company runs on Google. Where can they look?
explanation: The Ads Transparency Center lets anyone search by advertiser or website name to see the ads they run.

source.title: My Ad Center Help: About advertiser verification

prompt: You add new keywords and don't pick a match type. Which one do they get?
explanation: Broad match is the default because it reaches the widest range of searches. Pick phrase or exact if you want tighter control.

source.title: Google Ads Help: About keyword matching options

prompt: A florist adds 'flowers' as a negative keyword. Can their ad still show for 'red flower'?
options: Only if the ad is a Shopping ad
explanation: Negative keywords don't stretch to plurals or close variants, so add singular, plural and synonym versions yourself.

source.title: Google Ads Help: About negative keywords

prompt: Someone clicks the image in your Search ad. How is that click charged?
options: A flat fee per image view
explanation: Image clicks cost the same as a click on your text headline, so they're simply another way into your site.

source.title: Google Ads Help: About image assets for Search campaigns

prompt: A tour company targets Chicago with default location options. Who can see the ads?
options: People in or interested in Chicago
explanation: By default Google includes people in your area and people showing interest in it. Switch to 'Presence' to reach only locals.

source.title: Google Ads Help: About advanced location options

prompt: A gift shop wants Maximize conversions bidding. What must be set up first?
explanation: This strategy chases conversions, so Google needs conversion tracking to know what a win looks like.

source.title: Google Ads Help: About Maximize conversions bidding

prompt: You set a $20 target CPA. What happens with the cost of each single conversion?
explanation: Target CPA aims for an average. Individual conversions can land above or below your target.

source.title: Google Ads Help: About Target CPA bidding

prompt: You never change the conversion window on a Search campaign. How long is it by default?
explanation: Search and Display use a 30-day window by default. You can set it anywhere from 1 to 90 days to fit your sales cycle.

source.title: Google Ads Help: About conversion windows

prompt: A dentist completes advertiser verification. What shows in the ad disclosure afterwards?
explanation: Verified advertisers get an ad disclosure with their name and location, which helps people trust who's behind the ad.

source.title: Google Advertising Policies: Advertiser verification

prompt: Your ad's status reads 'Eligible (limited)'. What does that mean?
options: It has run out of budget
explanation: 'Eligible (limited)' means the ad can run, but policy limits where, for example by location, device or age.

source.title: Google Ads Help: Fix a disapproved ad or appeal a policy decision

prompt: A shop writes 'F-R-E-E delivery' in its headline to stand out. What's the issue?
options: It just costs more per click
explanation: Google's editorial rules don't allow gimmicky spellings like 'f-r-e-e'. Plain, clear wording keeps ads approved.

source.title: Google Advertising Policies: Google Ads policies

prompt: Your ad sends people to a page that says 'Under construction'. Can the ad run?
options: Yes, if the ad says 'coming soon'
explanation: Pages that are still under construction don't meet destination requirements. Finish the page before you advertise it.

source.title: Google Advertising Policies: Google Ads policies

prompt: An online casino wants to run Google Ads. What must its landing page show?
explanation: Gambling ads need approved countries, responsible gambling info on the landing page, and must never target minors.

source.title: Google Advertising Policies: Google Ads policies

prompt: You have 5 campaign-level callouts and 1 ad group callout. Which can serve in that ad group?
explanation: The more specific level wins. Once an ad group has its own callout, the campaign-level callouts don't show there.

source.title: Google Ads Help: About callout assets

prompt: A rival uses your brand name in their ad text. When do Google's trademark rules kick in?
options: Only if they also use your logo
explanation: Google's trademark rules for ads apply only after the trademark owner files a valid complaint, so brands need to act.

source.title: Google Advertising Policies: Google Ads policies

prompt: You set +50% for France and +100% for Paris. Which applies to a searcher in Paris?
explanation: When locations overlap, only the most specific one counts. A searcher in Paris gets just the Paris adjustment.

source.title: Google Ads Help: About bid adjustments

prompt: Google plans to suspend you for a less serious violation. How much warning should you get?

source.title: Google Advertising Policies: What happens if you violate our policies

prompt: Your keyword's Quality Score rises from 5 to 8. Is that score used directly in the ad auction?
options: Yes, it sets your exact price
Yes, it's the main auction input
No, it isn't an auction input
